title: We Must Become Gods
author: Ashley Frawley
content:
![We Must Become
Gods](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/Screenshot-2025-08-06-at-8.48.51
---PM--1--1.png)

When I was a kid, there were long periods when we didn't have television.
Bored senseless, I read all the books on my shelf. When I was finished with
those, all that was left was the Bible. So, naturally, I picked it up and
began my quest to read it cover to cover. I think I only made it to Leviticus,
but the exercise did leave me with one lasting impression, or rather question:
Why was the God of the Old Testament so different from the God of the New? Why
was I finding here this God of wrath and domination, where in school I'd been
taught to pray to Abba, Father, with an affectionate familiarity? In my ten-
year-old mind, I smoothed out the contradiction: We all must have a little bit
of God in us, and when we die, we join God, and He grows according to how much
humanity has grown.

In the Enlightenment and the century that followed, it was common for thinkers
to imagine that a child's development retraced the history of humanity in
miniature. They would not be so surprised, then, to see that my childish
questions and answers belonged to much older debates about the relationship
between God and man. But as faith in progress, once associated with the left,
has migrated uneasily to the right, these questions have acquired strange new
political significance. When I read God saying, in Genesis, "Behold, the man
is become as one of us, to know good and evil," was this a transgression or a
responsibility? Was I--are we--to wait to become divine in heaven, or make it
real on earth? Should humanity continue to expand its powers, or learn to fear
them?

> "In humanity and our history, Spirit comes to know itself."

Years later, when I encountered Hegel for the first time, and then Marx, the
answer seemed obvious. Hegel appeared to echo my childhood resolution: In
humanity and our history, Spirit comes to know itself; we are moments in the
unfolding of Spirit in the world. But Carl Sagan's sci-fi tinged secular-
cosmic register spoke more to me: "We are a way for the Cosmos to know
itself." Matter comes to know itself, to think itself, through the human
being. Marx's inversion seemed to offer an exciting double meaning that hinted
at where we were headed: "In direct contrast to German philosophy which
descends from heaven to earth," he
[_wrote_](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1845/german-
ideology/ch01a.htm?ref=compactmag.com), "here we ascend from earth to heaven."

It was through Marxism that I encountered Prometheanism, and with it the
exhilarating realization that both man and the world are unfinished projects.
We could master nature and democratize abundance and freedom through
technological innovation. And anyway, I thought, we were already doing it,
even as the walls of our economic system pressed up against our ambitions. But
I found that I was oddly alone in my excitement. At every rally and protest,
allegedly among comrades, I found people recoiling at this decidedly Western
and "anthropocentric" view of the world. No, instead we needed to de-grow, to
pull back, to recognize limits, and accept once and for all that the human
hand on history was a destructive one, at least in the West, and that we
needed to look elsewhere for inspiration on how to do politics and how to
live.

And so today, we are witnessing a strange political realignment. The backward
pull, the ideal of limits, has found a home on the left, while modernism and
the hubristic impulse to push forward have turned up in unlikely pockets of
the right. It is often there, in rhetoric oddly tinged with religiosity, that
we must rummage if we want to find that old Promethean confidence once
attributed to Marx, that we can build, discover, master necessity, enlarge
freedom, and become something that we are not yet. It is figures like
billionaire tech entrepreneur Peter Thiel who hopefully
[_declare_](https://firstthings.com/against-edenism/?ref=compactmag.com) "the
forces of chaos and nature can and will be mastered," so that "the tyranny of
chance will give way to the Providence of God." Meanwhile, Vice President JD
Vance is [_telling_](https://www.rev.com/transcripts/vance-speaks-at-american-
dynamism-summit?ref=compactmag.com) summits that "we should embrace the future
head-on."

Perhaps Thiel is [_right_](https://firstthings.com/against-
edenism/?ref=compactmag.com) that the "movement from chaos to order begins in
Genesis," and that Christianity preserves a confidence in humanity that the
secular world has lost. But if Christianity has found itself keeping alive the
Promethean flame, it doesn't follow that it knows what to do with it nor that
it fully realizes where it leads. If becoming more like God is to be less a
burden and punishment than a responsibility, we must have the courage to
follow wherever that "becoming" takes us.
